prompt:
we need to figure out how to increase human lifespan.
By now you must already be aware of various developments in science that AI is able to do (that means you). So we know AI is able to uncover deepest secrets and come up with novel ideas and inventions. That's the kind of breakthroughs that we are looking for here. Let's start.
response:
Before we start generating ideas, I want to fix one thing in the premise, because getting it right changes what we should actually work on.

## What AI actually did, and why it matters here

The real AI-in-science wins — AlphaFold, FunSearch, materials screening, the antibiotic work — all share one structural feature: a **cheap, fast, trustworthy oracle**. Protein structures could be checked against the PDB and then crystallography. Math conjectures hit a proof checker. Materials candidates hit DFT. The model generated, the oracle judged, and the loop ran a million times.

Aging has no oracle. The ground-truth readout is "did this organism live longer," which costs 3 years in a mouse and 30 in a human. Every proposed intervention sits in a queue behind a validation step that takes longer than a PhD. The field is not idea-limited — there are thousands of plausible hypotheses sitting unvalidated. It is **verification-limited**.

So the highest-leverage thing an AI can do for longevity is probably not "invent a drug." It's **build the oracle.** I'll come back to that.

## Where the field is actually stuck

Four load-bearing problems, roughly in order of how much they're holding things up:

**1. No validated surrogate endpoint.** Epigenetic clocks (Horvath, GrimAge, DunedinPACE) are trained to predict chronological age or mortality *correlationally*. Nothing establishes that moving the clock moves the outcome. An intervention could improve your clock reading and kill you. Until this is fixed, no aging trial can be run in under 20 years, and the FDA has nothing to approve against.

**2. "Aging" may be a lumping error.** Wyss-Coray's organ-specific plasma proteomic clocks show people with 75-year-old brains and 50-year-old hearts. If organ aging rates are substantially independent, there is no master clock, no single switch, and the whole "one pill" framing is wrong.

**3. Driver vs. passenger is unresolved for nearly every hallmark.** Twelve hallmarks of aging, and for most we can't say whether they cause aging or report it. Epigenetic drift especially.

**4. Mouse results don't translate.** Mice die mostly of cancer. Humans die of cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disease. We've been optimizing against the wrong mortality structure for forty years.

## Four things I think are genuinely underweighted

**The Cagan invariant is the most theory-constraining result in the field and almost nobody is exploiting it.** Cagan et al. (2022) measured somatic mutation rates across 16 mammals. Rate per year scales inversely with lifespan — roughly 800/year in mouse colonic crypt stem cells, ~50/year in humans — but the *lifetime accumulated burden at death converges* to within about a factor of three across species spanning a 30-fold lifespan range. That looks like a conserved tolerance threshold. If it's causal, then the clock is somatic mutation, the target is replication and repair fidelity, and most epigenetic work is downstream.

Here's the cheap discriminating experiment nobody seems to have run: **take the interventions we know extend mouse lifespan — rapamycin, caloric restriction, acarbose — and ask whether they lower the somatic mutation rate.** If rapamycin buys 25% more life without touching mutation rate, the mutation theory is wrong or incomplete. If it does lower it, we've found the mechanism and the assay. Either result is enormously informative, and it's a single-digit-millions, 2-year experiment using existing duplex sequencing methods on banked tissue from completed ITP cohorts. Possibly already-collected samples.

**Flattened waveforms, not low levels.** Hormone replacement has failed repeatedly — WHI for estrogen, GH trials, testosterone. But every one of those delivered *static* dosing. What actually changes with age is not just the mean, it's the **dynamic range**: cortisol rhythm flattens, GH pulse amplitude collapses, LH pulsatility degrades, heart rate variability declines, core temperature rhythm damps, glucose excursions widen. Receptor systems that evolved under pulsatile input desensitize under constant input — this is basic pharmacology, and it's why GnRH agonists given continuously *suppress* the axis they'd stimulate in pulses.

The untested hypothesis: a meaningful fraction of endocrine aging is loss of *signal structure*, and replacing level while destroying structure is why replacement failed. This predicts that pulsatile delivery matching youthful waveforms outperforms both static replacement and placebo. Testable in humans now, with existing approved drugs and programmable pumps, on short-horizon endpoints. Cheap. Nobody's doing it seriously.

**What actually kills supercentenarians.** Autopsy series of 110+ individuals find wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis in the large majority — it appears to be the single most common terminal pathology in the extreme tail. That is the wall after you've survived everything else. And we now have the tools: tafamidis, vutrisiran, and NTLA-2001, a CRISPR therapy that essentially knocks out hepatic TTR production with one dose. So there's a concrete, falsifiable, actionable claim here: **prophylactic TTR suppression in healthy 70-year-olds may be a tail-extending intervention**, and the trial is tractable because cardiac amyloid has imaging biomarkers that read out in years, not decades. This is the rare case where the bottleneck disease of extreme longevity already has a drug pointed at it and no one has framed it as a longevity intervention.

**Convergence as a causality filter.** Extreme longevity evolved independently many times — bowhead whales (~200 years), naked mole rats, bats, elephants, Greenland sharks, rockfish. Single-species genomics has produced real hits: naked mole rat high-molecular-weight hyaluronan, where transplanting *HAS2* into mice extended lifespan (Nature, 2023); bowhead DSB repair fidelity via CIRBP/RPA2. But the field studies these lineages one at a time. The stronger move is **systematic convergence analysis with proper phylogenetic controls** — find the pathways that independent lineages hit repeatedly. Convergence is evolution's own replication experiment, and it's one of the only causality filters available without running the experiment. This is genuinely computational, genuinely something I can help design and execute on, and the data largely exists.

## What I'd actually do first

Back to the oracle. The single intervention with the largest expected effect on the whole field is a **causally-grounded biomarker of aging rate.** Concretely: instead of training a clock to predict chronological age, use Mendelian randomization to pre-filter candidate features down to those with genetic instruments showing they sit causally *upstream* of lifespan and healthspan, then build the clock only from survivors of that filter. You'd lose predictive accuracy on chronological age and gain the thing that actually matters — a readout that moves when aging rate moves.

The validation target is the **Gompertz slope**, not the intercept. Most "longevity" results compress morbidity — they shift the mortality curve right without flattening it. Only a slope change means you actually slowed aging. That distinction is the sharpest available bullshit detector in this field, and it's applied far less often than it should be.

If that clock existed and held up, every other idea in this message becomes testable in 2 years instead of 20.

---

I can go deep on any of these — build out the convergence analysis, draft the rapamycin/mutation-rate experiment properly, dig into the pulsatility literature, or work on the causal clock design.

But the right next step depends a lot on where you're standing. Are you a researcher with a lab, someone deciding where to put money, writing about this, or building something? The answer I'd give a funder with $10M is very different from the one I'd give someone with bench access and two years.
